abstract: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) profoundly remodel microglial states, yet how the heterogeneity of disease-associated microglia (DAM) relates to neurodegeneration remains incompletely understood. Using a progranulin (PGRN) and TMEM106B-deficient mouse model recapitulating key features of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), including lysosomal impairment, we demonstrated that CSF1R inhibition reduced microgliosis yet accelerated neurodegeneration, suggesting a protective microglia contribution under lysosomal stress. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed that increasing Gpnmb expression within DAM was associated with a shift from immune and inflammatory processes toward a lysosomal, autolysosomal, and lipid-catabolic program. Across disease models, engagement of the GPNMB-associated program correlated with neurodegeneration. Consistently, A{beta}-driven models with limited neurodegeneration exhibited prominent DAM activation but comparatively limited GPNMB expression and engagement of this program. The GPNMB-associated program was TREM2-dependent, while loss of TREM2 signaling under lysosomal stress was associated with exacerbated neuronal damage. Conversely, lysosomal rescue markedly reduced the GPNMB-associated program, demonstrating its reversibility. CSF proteomics identified a convergent lysosomal and microglial signature across models overlapping with alterations reported in human FTD. Together, GPNMB marks reversible, TREM2-regulated lysosomal transcriptional adaptation along the DAM continuum that scales with lysosomal burden and neurodegenerative severity, consistent with a potentially protective microglial response under lysosomal stress.
